title: XENON experiment finds quietest neutrinos ever detected
excerpt: Ultra-sensitive detector designed by UChicago team to search for dark matter captures elusive low-energy neutrino particles from the sun
content:
Ultra-sensitive detector designed by UChicago team to search for dark matter captures elusive low-energy neutrino particles from the sun

Buried deep in an Italian mountain, an experiment known as XENON has picked up the quietest signatures of neutrinos ever detected. 

Originally designed to look for hints of the mysterious substance known as dark matter, the detector’s extraordinary sensitivity allowed it to capture a different target—the elusive particle known as the neutrino. Neutrinos are constantly flying off the surface of the sun, with a range of different energies. The XENON experiment was able to capture neutrinos traveling at extremely low energies, lower than anything previously detected.

“This opens up possibilities for new explorations of neutrinos and their behavior,” said Luca Grandi, professor of physics at the University of Chicago, who led the design and construction of the latest iteration of the XENON experiment, known as XENONnT. 

Neutrinos, sometimes called “ghost particles,” are thought to hold the key to many questions about the universe. They are difficult to study, however, because they only rarely interact with the matter that makes up our world; experiments must painstakingly filter out all other background noise. 

The finding shows that XENONnT has achieved such a low background, Grandi said, “that we are becoming an observatory for rare processes, which can contribute to multiple fields of particle physics.” 

Extraordinary sensitivity

XENONnT is located 4,600 feet deep into the sedimentary rock of central Italy’s Gran Sasso mountain, which shields it from stray cosmic rays or other phenomena that could interfere with the readings. 

The experiment consists of detectors set into a large tank filled with six tons of pure xenon. Most particles are stopped by the mountain and thick walls—except for the most elusive particles, like dark matter or neutrinos. If one of these happens to bump into a xenon atom inside the tank, the detector picks up the shock waves from the collision. Every part of the setup is rigorously designed and fabricated with ultra-pure materials to reduce background noise so that these miniscule signatures can be detected.

This allowed XENONnT to capture signatures from solar neutrinos traveling with energies down to just 17 kilo electron-volts (keV)—far less than the energy of a flying mosquito. 

Previously, other experiments could only detect solar neutrinos with much higher energies, around 200 keV. 

“We are adding a large chunk of sensitivity to this field,” said Grandi. “It’s very cool that XENON was able to say something new about neutrinos, even though it is much smaller than most neutrino experiments.” 

Grandi noted the data analyzed came from only the first phase of XENONnT. The detector has since been upgraded, and the forthcoming data should provide a further window on the results.

A busy week for xenon detectors 

The day after the XENONnT announced its low-energy neutrino detection, a competitor experiment in South Dakota, known as the LZ Dark Matter Experiment, reported the detection of an anomalous interaction in their detector. 

It’s possible this could be a signal from dark matter, but science must first rule out every possible mundane explanation, such as background noise produced by something else in the experiment.

"We are extremely well positioned," said Grandi, "to test the origin of this excess event, trying to distinguish between the hypothesis that such a high-energy interaction might be due to a dark matter particle interacting inelastically with xenon atoms, and the hypothesis that this is simply a yet-unexplained background that might be present in LZ but not in our detector."

The collaborations of both XENONnT and the LZ Dark Matter Experiment are also planning for the next-generation XLZD experiment, which aims to extend the search for dark matter to the highest sensitivities ever achieved. 

XLZD could also measure low-energy solar neutrinos with exceptional precision, while opening new opportunities in neutrino physics and studies of other extremely rare processes.

“This observation of low-energy solar neutrinos demonstrates how advances driven by the search for dark matter are opening entirely new windows on the universe,” said Elena Aprile, professor at Columbia University and spokesperson of the XENON Collaboration. “It shows that technologies originally developed to observe some of the rarest interactions in nature are now enabling us to explore fundamental questions well beyond their original scientific goals.”

Citation: “First Measurement of Solar Neutrinos through Elastic Neutrino-Electron Scattering at the keV Scale.” XENON Collaboration, posted to arXiv Sept. 1, 2026.
